readerTitle: A reorg doesn't remove problems. It moves them.
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (식자재·생활용품 유통사, 레스토랑 4곳 운영사) + 가상 적용 (소프트웨어 회사) + 출처가 잘못 알려진 인용 일화
insight: 모든 조직 구조에는 이음새(팀 사이의 경계)가 있다. 재편은 이음새를 없애지 못하고 옮길 뿐이므로, 가장 중요한 협업을 팀 안으로 넣고 새로 생기는 이음새를 미리 관리할 때만 효과가 있다.
misconception: 성과가 나쁘면 조직을 새로 짜는 것이 가장 확실한 해결책이고, 재편을 자주 할수록 변화에 빨리 대응하는 조직이다.

sources.text: 조직 설계의 일반 원리 (팀 경계와 조정 비용, 재편에 따른 전환 비용)
유통사, 레스토랑 운영사, 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 모두 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 'We trained hard... reorganized' 인용문은 흔히 로마 작가 페트로니우스의 말로 알려져 있지만 그의 저작에서는 확인되지 않으며 20세기에 만들어진 것으로 보입니다. 카드에는 출처가 잘못 알려진 문장이라고 명시했습니다. 게시 전 인용 출처 연구 자료로 다시 확인하세요.
재편 후 생산성 저하, 핵심 인력 이탈 같은 전환 비용은 일반적인 설명으로만 적었고 구체적인 비율이나 연구 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 수치를 추가하려면 1차 출처를 확인해야 합니다.

cards.title: A reorg doesn't remove problems. It moves them.
body: Two businesses redrew their org charts in the same month. One was a distributor. The other ran four restaurants.
A year later, the distributor had fixed the problem it set out to fix. The restaurant group still had its old problem, plus some new ones. Both teams had worked just as hard.

image.label: Two org charts being redrawn side by side
image.brief: 두 장의 조직도를 나란히 놓고 각각 손이 박스와 선을 다시 그리는 장면. 왼쪽 배경에는 창고 선반과 상자, 오른쪽 배경에는 주방 화구와 냄비. 따뜻한 플랫 일러스트. 실제 기업 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your biggest customers are unhappy.
body: You run a distributor with three regional warehouses. Each region buys, prices and invoices on its own. Your national grocery chains complain: three prices, three invoices, three contacts.
You decide to reorganize. What should you settle first?

options.text: The new org chart, so people stop worrying about their jobs
options.feedback: Speed does reduce anxiety. But a chart drawn before the problem is named often just reshuffles the same seams.

options.text: The one problem the reorg must fix, and which handoffs will get harder
options.feedback: This takes longer up front, but it tells you what to put inside one team and what new friction to plan for.

options.text: Ask each region head to propose a structure
options.feedback: You get buy-in, but each head will tend to protect their own region. And the regions are where the customer's pain starts.

cards.title: Same move, different results.
body: **The distributor** named its problem: national chains had to deal with three separate regions. It formed one national accounts team with one price list and one invoice. It knew a new seam would appear between that team and the warehouses, so it set a weekly rule for who gets stock first.

**The restaurant group** saw profits fall and moved buying and hiring from each restaurant's manager to a central office. It never asked why profits fell. The real cause was one weak manager at one site. Now every chef waited on central buying, and that site was still weak.

image.label: Two timelines: one problem solved, one problem moved
image.brief: 좌우 두 개의 타임라인. 왼쪽(유통사): 문제 하나에 체크 표시, 새로 생긴 작은 이음새에 '주간 규칙' 메모. 오른쪽(레스토랑): 원래 문제(빨간 점)가 그대로 있고 새 빨간 점 두 개가 추가됨. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Every structure has seams
body: A **reorganization** changes who reports to whom and which work sits together in the same team.

Work inside a team is easy to coordinate: one boss, shared goals, daily contact. Work that crosses teams is slower. Every structure has these **seams**. A reorg can't remove them. It can only move them.
So the useful question isn't which chart looks best. It's which coordination matters most right now. Put that inside one team, and decide how you'll manage the seams you're creating.

image.label: A seam moving from one place on an org chart to another
image.brief: 조직도 두 개를 전후 비교. '전': 고객 응대가 세 지역 박스 사이 점선 경계를 가로지름. '후': 고객 응대가 한 박스 안으로 들어가고, 대신 새 점선 경계가 그 박스와 창고 박스 사이에 생김. 경계선은 주황색으로 강조.

cards.title: Reorgs have a price, paid up front.
body: Even a good reorg costs something before it pays off.
Pay that price only for a problem that structure can actually fix.
list: **New bosses:** people spend weeks learning what their new manager wants
**Broken networks:** the informal "I'll just call Maria" links get cut
**Stalled decisions:** nobody is sure who decides, so many things wait
**Departures:** good people may leave while things are uncertain

cards.title: Some problems only look structural.
body: A weak manager, an unclear strategy, or pay that rewards the wrong thing will survive any new chart. The restaurant group moved boxes around a people problem.

A quick test: **imagine your best people in the old structure.** Would the problem still be there? If yes, the structure may be the cause. If no, fix the people, the goals or the incentives first. It's cheaper and faster.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams often reorganize into product squads when the real issue is unclear priorities. The squads then inherit the same fight over what to build first.

cards.title: Frequent reorgs become the problem.
body: A line often credited to the Roman writer Petronius says: *"We trained hard, but every time we were beginning to form into teams, we would be reorganized."* It doesn't appear in his writings and was probably written in the 20th century. It survives because it feels true.

Each reorg resets relationships and habits. Do too many and teams never settle long enough to work well. When you do reorganize, decide quickly and announce it clearly. A long stretch of rumors costs more than the change itself.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your 60-person company is organized by function: engineering, design, sales, support. New customers churn in their first month because setup is confusing. Sales promises it, support fixes it, product owns the screens. Nobody owns the result.
Your CEO proposes reorganizing everyone into product squads. What do you suggest?

options.text: Go ahead with the full squad reorg
options.feedback: It might help, but it moves every seam in the company to fix one. You pay the full transition cost, and onboarding could still fall between squads.

options.text: Form one small onboarding team with a single owner, drawn from support, product and engineering
options.feedback: It puts the one broken handoff inside one team and leaves the rest alone. You'll need to agree how this team gets engineering time.

options.text: Keep the structure and add a weekly onboarding meeting
options.feedback: Cheap and fast, and it helps people talk. But a meeting shares the problem without giving anyone ownership of it.

cards.title: Reorganize to fix one named problem, and plan for the new seams.
body: A new structure puts some work together and pushes other work apart. Choose what belongs together on purpose, and check that the problem is really about structure.
**Try it today:** name the handoff in your business that fails most often. Is it inside one team, or across a seam?
